rewritten_text:
After seeing our friend safely settled in his new office, we turned our thoughts toward Windsor. It was so close to London that leaving Raymond and Perdita did not feel like a painful separation. We said goodbye at the Protector's Palace. It was pleasant to watch my sister enter into the spirit of her role and try to fill it with suitable dignity. More than ever, her inward pride struggled with her modest manner. Her shyness was real: like Raymond, she feared being undervalued and slighted by the world. But Perdita thought about other people more often than he did. Part of her embarrassment came from wanting to spare those around her any sense of inferiority, a distinction she herself never thought of making. Idris's birth and upbringing would have prepared her better for formal ceremonies. Yet their very familiarity made them tedious to her, while Perdita, despite every difficulty, plainly enjoyed her position. Her mind was too full of new ideas for our departure to hurt much. She said goodbye affectionately and promised to visit soon, but she did not regret the circumstances that were separating us. Raymond's excitement knew no bounds. He scarcely knew what to do with his new power. His head overflowed with plans, though he had chosen none yet. Still, he promised himself, his friends, and the world that his time as Protector would be marked by some achievement of extraordinary glory. We discussed them and reflected on their situation as our smaller party returned to Windsor Castle. We were delighted to escape the turmoil of politics and welcomed our quiet life with fresh enthusiasm. There was plenty to occupy us, but I now directed my restless energy entirely toward intellectual work. Hard study proved an excellent remedy for the agitation that would certainly have troubled me if I had remained idle. Perdita had allowed Clara to return to Windsor with us. She and my own two lovely babies gave us endless interest and amusement.

Only Adrian's health disturbed our peace. It was clearly growing worse, but there were no definite symptoms to identify the illness. His unusually bright eyes, lively expression, and flushed cheeks did make us fear consumption. Yet he felt neither pain nor fear himself. He devoted himself eagerly to his books and rested from study with his favourite companions, his sister and me.

Ten minutes later, Lord Arthur Savile rushed out of Bentinck House, his face white with terror and his eyes wild with grief. He forced his way through the fur-coated footmen gathered around the large striped awning, apparently seeing and hearing nothing. The night was bitterly cold. Gas lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind, but his hands were feverishly hot and his forehead burned. He went on and on, staggering almost like a drunken man. A policeman watched him curiously as he passed. A beggar shuffled from an archway to ask for money, then drew back in fear at the sight of misery greater than his own. Once, Arthur stopped under a lamp and stared at his hands. He thought he could already see bloodstains on them, and a faint cry escaped his trembling lips.

Murder! That was what the palm reader had seen. Murder! The night itself seemed to know, and the lonely wind howled the word into his ear. It filled the streets' dark corners. It grinned down at him from the rooftops.

First he reached the Park, where the dark trees seemed to draw him in. He leaned wearily against the railings, cooling his forehead on the wet metal and listening to the trembling silence among the trees. 'Murder! Murder!' he repeated, as if saying it often enough might weaken the word's horror. His own voice made him shudder, yet he almost wished its echo would wake the sleeping city. He felt a wild urge to stop a passing stranger and confess everything.

Then he crossed Oxford Street and wandered into narrow, disreputable alleys. Two women with painted faces jeered at him as he went by. Swearing and the sounds of blows came from a dark courtyard, followed by piercing screams. On a damp doorstep he saw poor, elderly people huddled together, their backs bent. A strange pity filled him. Were these children of sin and suffering doomed to their fate, just as he was to his? Were they too merely puppets in some monstrous performance?

What struck him was not suffering's mystery but its absurdity: its complete uselessness, its grotesque lack of meaning. Nothing seemed connected; nothing fit together. He was astonished by the clash between the age's shallow optimism and the actual conditions of life. He was still very young.

Eventually he found himself outside Marylebone Church. The silent road looked like a long strip of polished silver, marked here and there with elaborate dark patterns of moving shadow.

"And think of this, ma'am," Oliver said, tears gathering despite his efforts to hold them back. "Think how young and kind she is, and how much joy and comfort she brings everyone around her. I'm sure—certain—completely certain—that for your sake, because you're so good yourself, and for her own sake, and for all the people she makes happy, she won't die. Heaven would never let her die so young."

"Hush," Mrs. Maylie said, placing her hand on Oliver's head. "You think as a child does, poor boy. Nevertheless, you remind me of my duty. I forgot it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I can be forgiven. I am old, and I have seen enough sickness and death to know the agony of being separated from those we love. I have also seen enough to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are left to those who love them. Yet this should offer comfort in our sorrow. Heaven is just, and such losses teach us profoundly that a brighter world exists beyond this one, and that the journey to it is swift. God's will be done! I love her, and He knows how much!"

Oliver was surprised to see Mrs. Maylie bring her grieving under control as she spoke, apparently with a single effort. She straightened herself and became calm and determined. He was more astonished still to discover that her determination held. Through all the nursing and watching that followed, she remained ready and composed, attending steadily to every responsibility that had fallen to her and even appearing cheerful. But he was young and did not know what strong minds can achieve under difficult circumstances. How could he, when the people who possess them so seldom know themselves?

A night of anxiety followed. By morning, Mrs. Maylie's fears were all too clearly justified. Rose had entered the first stage of a high and dangerous fever.

"We must take action, Oliver, and not give in to useless grief," Mrs. Maylie said, touching a finger to her lips and looking steadily at him. "This letter must be sent to Mr. Losberne as quickly as possible. It must go to the market town, no more than four miles away by the footpath across the field. From there, a special messenger on horseback must take it straight to Chertsey. The people at the inn will arrange that, and I know I can trust you to make sure it happens."

Oliver could not answer, but his face showed how anxious he was to set off immediately.
